perDefect.matchedFinding: Server serialize() emits the US spelling "canceled" (single L) for sub.canceledAt truthy case, and also for sub.status when it presumably equals "cancelled" — but the documented contract requires the value "cancelled" (UK spelling, double L); the client's isCancelled() checks `sub.status === "cancelled"`, which will never match "canceled", so the cancelled banner never appears — this is the root cause of the QA bug.

Server returns `amount: sub.amountCents`, i.e. a cents-denominated integer, while the documented contract specifies `amount: number // dollars`; the client's formatAmount() does `sub.amount.toFixed(2)` assuming the value is already in dollars, so the displayed price will be shown as 100x too large (e.g. $1999.00 instead of $19.99) with no unit conversion anywhere in the pipeline.

There is no shared/generated type or schema (e.g. no shared TS interface, no OpenAPI/JSON-schema validation, no contract test) enforcing that server output matches the documented contract, so the spelling and units mismatches were not caught at compile time or by any automated check.

Server serializes cancelled subscriptions with status value "canceled" (US spelling, single L), but the documented contract's enum only contains "cancelled" (UK spelling, double L) — the server's own output is not a member of its documented enum.

Server returns amount: sub.amountCents (a cents value) while the documented contract specifies amount is in dollars; client's formatAmount() does `$${sub.amount.toFixed(2)}` assuming sub.amount is already dollars, so displayed amounts will be rendered 100x too large.

Server's serialize() emits the US spelling "canceled" (`sub.canceledAt ? "canceled" : sub.status`) while the documented contract and the client's isCancelled() both use the UK spelling "cancelled" (`sub.status === "cancelled"`). Because the server never emits the string "cancelled", isCancelled() is always false for every subscription, including ones with canceledAt set — this is the exact root cause of the QA-reported bug that the cancelled banner never appears.

Server's serialize() returns `amount: sub.amountCents` verbatim (a cents-denominated integer per its own field name) but the documented contract declares `amount: number // dollars`, and the client's formatAmount() trusts that contract, computing `$${sub.amount.toFixed(2)}` with no /100 conversion. This means any subscription amount will be displayed 100x too large (e.g. amountCents=1999 renders as "$1999.00" instead of "$19.99"), a second, independent violation of the documented contract that will silently corrupt every displayed price.

Server spells the cancelled status as "canceled" (US spelling, in serialize(): `sub.canceledAt ? "canceled" : sub.status`) while the client's isCancelled() does a strict equality check against "cancelled" (UK spelling, matching the documented contract). Because the server never emits the literal string "cancelled", isCancelled() returns false for every subscription regardless of actual cancellation state, which is the direct root cause of the banner never appearing — confirmed by the spelling called out in both code comments.

Independent of the status bug, the documented contract specifies `amount` as dollars, but serialize() returns `sub.amountCents` unconverted (no division by 100) under the `amount` key, and the client's formatAmount() does `$${sub.amount.toFixed(2)}` assuming the value is already dollars. This produces a dollar amount inflated 100x (e.g. 500 cents rendered as "$500.00" instead of "$5.00") for every subscription, not just cancelled ones — a second, separate contract violation with financial-display impact and broader reach than the banner bug.

genericSearch.ts's excludeDeleted() hardcodes the column name 'deleted_at', but the users table has no deleted_at column at all (only is_deleted BOOLEAN) — the exclusion filter can never match anything on 'users'.

Because the ORM is configured with unknownColumnMode: 'silent-skip', the where('deleted_at', 'IS', null) clause against the users table is silently dropped instead of erroring, so search('users', …) runs with no soft-delete filter whatsoever — this is the direct cause of deleted accounts appearing in search results.

Nothing in the described system (types, tests, schema validation, or the query builder) enforces that excludeDeleted() references a column that actually exists on the target table, so the same class of bug (filter silently no-ops due to column mismatch) can recur for any other filter, not just deleted_at.

Because unknownColumnMode is 'silent-skip', the query builder silently drops the deleted_at clause when it runs against users instead of raising an error, so no soft-delete filter is applied to user search at all — this is the direct mechanism causing deleted accounts to leak into results while orders (which does have deleted_at) is correctly filtered.

No try/catch/finally around `await refreshToken(oldToken)` (lines 19-21 of tokenService.js): if `api.post('/auth/refresh', ...)` rejects (network error, 5xx, timeout), the exception propagates up uncaught and `refreshing` is never reset to `false`. Every subsequent `getToken()` call then permanently falls into the 'wait a bit and use whatever we have' branch, forever returning the same stale `currentToken` (or `null`) — a single failed refresh permanently breaks the client until a full page reload.

Worse than merely 'stale': per the code comment, 'the server invalidates oldToken the moment it receives this request' — so as soon as the refreshing call's POST lands, `currentToken` (still holding the old value) is guaranteed-revoked server-side, not just close to expiry. Any concurrent caller that reads `currentToken` in that window (either via the sleep(50) branch or via the initiating call's own in-flight requests started before refresh) will deterministically get a 401, not just probabilistically.

The 'someone else is refreshing' branch (`await sleep(50); return currentToken;`) is a single fixed-duration poll, not a loop or a subscription to the in-flight refresh. If the actual `/auth/refresh` round-trip takes longer than 50ms (entirely plausible on a slow network, which is exactly when refreshes matter most), the waiting caller returns before `currentToken` has been updated, handing back an expired/invalid token to its caller and causing the downstream authenticated request to fail with a spurious 401.

Concurrent requests already using the current token race against a parallel refresh: refreshToken() invalidates oldToken server-side 'the moment it receives the request', but since every call site invokes getToken() independently with no shared request queue, any request already in flight (or dispatched moments later) with that same token gets rejected once the refresh lands — this is the direct mechanism behind the reported intermittent logouts.

Data residency is enforced by regional data domiciling, not application-level filtering: each tenant is assigned a home region (US or EU) at provisioning time, and that tenant's document content, CRDT operation log, and audit log are stored and processed exclusively on infrastructure physically located in that region.

Use CRDTs (e.g. Yjs/Automerge-style RGA or Peritext for rich text) rather than centralized Operational Transformation, because CRDTs guarantee mathematically that concurrent edits converge without a single serializing authority, which is what makes zero-data-loss merging survive a regional outage instead of just a network blip.

Regional collaboration servers are relay/persistence nodes, not merge arbiters: they append incoming CRDT updates to a durable per-document operation log and fan them out to other connected clients, while the actual conflict-free merge happens independently on each replica — this keeps the server simple and avoids making it a single point of correctness failure.
